title: Only 31% of Federal Leaders Can See Their Shadow AI
summary: The Department of Homeland Security recently ordered civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek products from their systems, including certain third-party
body_markdown:
The Department of Homeland Security recently


[ordered civilian agencies](https://cyberscoop.com/dhs-bans-deepseek-federal-agencies/) to remove DeepSeek products from their systems, including certain third-party products built using its technology. For federal cybersecurity leaders, the order raises a practical question: Can you identify where a prohibited AI tool is being used, what data it can access, and whether security policies are being enforced?


For many agencies, the answer is far from clear. In fact, in a


[May 2026 survey](https://www.netskope.com/resources/reports-guides/operationalizing-zero-trust-for-the-federal-government-in-the-age-of-ai) of 275 federal civilian and defense IT and security leaders, conducted by Market Connections and sponsored by Netskope, only 31% reported high or complete visibility into public AI tools and shadow AI activity. Another 33% described their visibility as limited or nonexistent.


As agencies expand AI adoption, finding prohibited tools is the first step. The harder work is understanding how AI interacts with sensitive data and whether security controls work across those interactions.


## AI risk is moving beyond the chatbot


Employees using personal AI accounts are a familiar concern, but some of the harder risks to detect don’t involve a chatbot.


Consider a hypothetical federal contracting office using an approved document platform that recently introduced AI-powered summarization. Employees begin using the feature to review vendor proposals containing procurement-sensitive pricing. The application is approved and the accounts are managed, so nothing looks wrong. But that approval doesn’t necessarily tell the security team what data the AI feature sends to a model, where that data is processed, or which controls apply.


The challenge extends to application programming interfaces (APIs), where applications exchange data with AI models, often without a user directly interacting with the model. Only


[24% of respondents](https://www.netskope.com/resources/reports-guides/operationalizing-zero-trust-for-the-federal-government-in-the-age-of-ai) reported high or complete visibility into API-based AI interactions.


The growing use of Model Context Protocol (MCP), which connects AI systems to external tools and data sources, adds another dimension. Netskope Threat Labs observed a 4x increase in enterprise MCP traffic over a 10 week period, illustrating how quickly new AI connections are expanding.


## Seeing AI isn’t the same as protecting the data


Discovering an AI application is only the beginning. Agencies also need to understand which accounts are being used, what information is being shared, and whether policies can prevent inappropriate access or disclosure. An agency can approve a cloud storage service and still have no idea when an employee uploads sensitive files to a personal account within it. AI works the same way: approving a tool says nothing about the account, the instance, or the data.


The research suggests a significant enforcement gap.


[Just 13%](https://www.netskope.com/resources/reports-guides/operationalizing-zero-trust-for-the-federal-government-in-the-age-of-ai) of respondents said their agencies apply security policy consistently across AI agents, applications, endpoints, cloud, and SaaS.


That gap matters as agencies implement federal AI requirements.


[OMB M-25-21](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/M-25-21-Accelerating-Federal-Use-of-AI-through-Innovation-Governance-and-Public-Trust.pdf) calls for AI use case inventories, governance, and risk management practices, but an inventory doesn’t automatically reveal every AI interaction or enforce controls over sensitive data.


The DeepSeek order brings the distinction into focus. Agencies need more than a list of prohibited products. They need ways to identify covered usage, assess exposure, and verify that appropriate controls are working. A ban sets the rule. Visibility and enforcement help agencies demonstrate that it’s being followed.


## Three questions federal security leaders should ask


Federal teams need a greater understanding of what their existing security controls can actually see and enforce.


1. Can we discover AI usage across approved and unapproved applications, embedded features, APIs, and agent connections?
2. Can we identify when sensitive data is involved, whether through a prompt, file upload, or application-to-model exchange?
3. Can we enforce policies consistently across those interactions and produce evidence of what happened, what account was involved, and whether a control worked?


A gap in any of these areas shows you where to start.


## From AI visibility to secure adoption


Agencies that can answer yes to those questions can show their CAIO, authorizing official, or inspector general where AI is running, what data it touches, and which controls apply. That’s the evidence AI governance under


[M-25-21](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/M-25-21-Accelerating-Federal-Use-of-AI-through-Innovation-Governance-and-Public-Trust.pdf) depends on, and it’s what most agencies in the survey don’t yet have.
